title: Abu Dharr
hook: plain speaker, critic of hoarded wealth, who walked alone and died alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Salman the Persian: the fire, the church, slavery, and Medina at last. Your line was the seeker. What question did you take one step further? Day eight hundred twenty-five.

An army is on the march, and one camel can't keep up. It's thin and slow, and its rider falls further and further behind, until the column is gone over the horizon. So he gets down, loads his things on his own back, and walks. Later, the people in camp see a figure coming along the road by himself. Someone says: there's a man walking alone. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: let it be Abu Dharr. It is. Today: Abu Dharr, the man who walked alone.
screen: `A CAMEL THAT CAN'T KEEP UP.` → `HE WALKS, CARRYING HIS THINGS.` → `LET IT BE ABU DHARR.`

segments.voice: The scene comes from Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet, on the road to Tabuk. When Abu Dharr reaches the camp, tradition says the Prophet spoke of him: may God have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, he will die alone, and he will be raised alone. Plain words, and Abu Dharr was a man of plain words. Bukhari keeps a report from late in his life. A visitor found him living out at al-Rabadha, and asked why. Abu Dharr explained. In Syria he had argued over a verse. In Pickthall's translation: "They who hoard up gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah", followed by a warning of a painful doom. The governor said the verse was about other people. Abu Dharr said: it's about us and them. The quarrel grew and reached the caliph in Medina, and in the end Abu Dharr settled out at al-Rabadha. And yet the same Abu Dharr was once corrected. In another report in Bukhari, he insulted a man by mocking his mother, and the Prophet told him plainly: you are a man with the ignorance of the old days still in you. Abu Dharr took it. Later, someone noticed that he and his servant wore matching cloaks, and asked why. He said the Prophet had taught: your servants are your brothers; feed them from what you eat, dress them from what you wear. So the plain speaker was corrected too, and he wore the correction, quite literally, on his servant's back. Tradition says he died at al-Rabadha, far from the city, with his wife beside him, and was buried by travelers who happened by. In his own telling at al-Rabadha, it was an argument about a verse that took him there.
screen: `HE WALKS ALONE, HE WILL DIE ALONE.` · `THE HOARDERS: US AND THEM.` · `CORRECTED, AND HE TOOK IT.` · `THE SERVANT DRESSED LIKE HIM.` · then, large: `WALKED ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak one plain truth kindly. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind something true you've been avoiding saying. To a friend, a parent, a manager, or to yourself. Find the plainest way to say it, in one sentence. Then dress it with care, the way Abu Dharr dressed his servant in what he wore himself: the same truth, given kindly. Say it silently once. If you pray, you can ask God for courage and gentleness together. If not, just hold the sentence and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Abu Dharr. A companion of plain words, who spoke against hoarded wealth, took correction, and walked alone. Today's word.
Your line: walked alone. Today, say one true thing you've been holding back, plainly and kindly, even if you're the only one saying it. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Dharr al-Ghifari as a companion known for honesty, simple living and concern for the poor, and his reports on treating servants as brothers are taught in lessons on character.

fork.setup: you're Abu Dharr, on the march, and your camel is too weak to keep up. the army is pulling away. what do you do?
options: wait for someone to come back for you.
load your things on your back and walk.
fork.reveal: he walked on alone, and when he reached the camp the Prophet said: may God have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone.

original.note: Arabic: Abu Dharr, the name by which the companion Jundub ibn Junadah is known.

trapdoor: what it means: a plain speaker whose honesty about wealth took him far from the city, and who learned to make plain words kind.
what a scholar hears: the Tabuk scene is in Ibn Ishaq; Bukhari keeps both his account of al-Rabadha and the dispute over 9:34, and the report of the matching cloaks.
recall: called the daughter of a Jew

notes: The Tabuk scene and the saying 'he walks alone, dies alone, is raised alone' are from Ibn Ishaq (via Ibn Hisham), not a sahih collection; framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
His death at al-Rabadha with his wife present and burial by passing travelers is from the sirah tradition; framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Bukhari 1406 and 30 numbering and paraphrases: confirm. The governor in Syria is Mu'awiyah; left unnamed deliberately to keep the focus.
Original note gives his given name as Jundub ibn Junadah: confirm.

Editor: review no longer recalls 'chains'; Bukhari 1406 summary corrected (the dispute went to Uthman in Medina before he settled at al-Rabadha) and uncited 'far from Medina' cut from teach and match; garbled practice simile rewritten.

Audit: cut the narrator's moral ('plainness has to be kind'), which Bukhari 30 does not teach (it is about not shaming a man's mother and treating servants as brothers), and the uncited 'it's where honest speech took him'; Bukhari 30 and 1406 speak of slaves (ghulam/khawal) where the script says servants: Keeper may prefer the plainer word.
